We want all \(f(x)\in \mathbb Z[x]\) such that

\[
\gcd\bigl(f(n),f(2^n)\bigr)=1
\]

for every natural number \(n\).

---

### 1. The constant term must be odd

Since \(2\equiv 0\pmod 2\), for any integer polynomial \(f\),

\[
f(2)\equiv f(0)\pmod 2,\qquad f(4)\equiv f(0)\pmod 2.
\]

If \(f(0)\) were even, then both \(f(2)\) and \(f(4)\) would be even. Taking \(n=2\), we would have

\[
2\mid f(2)\quad\text{and}\quad 2\mid f(2^2)=f(4),
\]

so \(f(2)\) and \(f(2^2)\) would not be coprime, a contradiction. Hence

\[
f(0)\ \text{is odd}.
\]

Therefore, for every \(m\ge 1\),

\[
f(2^m)\equiv f(0)\equiv 1\pmod 2,
\]

so each \(f(2^m)\) is odd.

---

### 2. No \(f(2^m)\) can have an odd prime divisor

Suppose, for some \(m\ge 1\), that an odd prime \(p\) divides \(f(2^m)\).

Let \(t\) be the multiplicative order of \(2\) modulo \(p\). Since \(p\) is odd, such a \(t\) exists, and \(t\mid p-1\), so \(\gcd(t,p)=1\).

By the Chinese remainder theorem, choose a positive integer \(n\) such that

\[
n\equiv m\pmod t
\]

and

\[
n\equiv 2^m\pmod p.
\]

Then:

- Since \(n\equiv 2^m\pmod p\),

\[
f(n)\equiv f(2^m)\equiv 0\pmod p.
\]

- Since \(n\equiv m\pmod t\), we have \(2^n\equiv 2^m\pmod p\). Hence

\[
f(2^n)\equiv f(2^m)\equiv 0\pmod p.
\]

Thus \(p\mid f(n)\) and \(p\mid f(2^n)\), contradicting the requirement that \(f(n)\) and \(f(2^n)\) are coprime.

So no odd prime can divide any \(f(2^m)\). But we already know \(f(2^m)\) is odd. Therefore,

\[
f(2^m)=\pm 1
\]

for every \(m\ge 1\).

---

### 3. \(f\) must be constant

If \(f\) were nonconstant, then \(|f(x)|\to\infty\) as \(x\to\infty\). In particular,

\[
|f(2^m)|\to\infty
\]

as \(m\to\infty\), contradicting the fact that \(f(2^m)=\pm1\) for all \(m\ge1\). Hence \(f\) must be constant.

Write \(f(x)=c\). Then for every \(n\),

\[
\gcd(f(n),f(2^n))=\gcd(c,c)=|c|.
\]

For this to equal \(1\), we need \(|c|=1\). Thus

\[
c=1\quad\text{or}\quad c=-1.
\]

Both constant polynomials clearly work.

\[
\boxed{f(x)=1 \text{ or } f(x)=-1}
\]
